newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israeli bonds end higher on May CPI.
newsitem.headline: Israeli bonds end higher on May CPI.

text.p: Israeli bonds closed higher on Monday led by unlinked bonds on expectations of a cut in interest rates because of the lower than expected May consumer price index (CPI), traders said.
Indices:
* Government bonds general: +0.07 pct to 107.22
* CPI-linked government bonds: +0.01 pct to 107.10
* Unlinked government bonds: +0.25 pct to 108.34
* Dollar-linked government bonds: +0.11 pct to 105.71
* Bank of Israel short-term Makam bills: +0.08 pct to 106.63
Volume including Makams was 120 million shekels.
"Unlinked bonds rose sharply today on expectations of a cut in interest rates because of the surprisingly low CPI," said an investment manager at Jerusalem Capital Markets.
The May CPI, published on Sunday after the end of the trading day, rose 0.5 percent, well under analysts' expectations of 0.7 to 0.9 percent.
The market was expecting a 0.3 to 0.5 percentage point cut in interest rates, the investment manager said.
The Bank of Israel will announce its July monetary programme including interest rates on June 23. The base rate has been unchanged at 13.9 percent since the end of February.

"Prices of short-term CPI-linked bonds are falling as a result of the low CPI," said a trader. "The price of these bonds had been higher for a short while because of the good yields, but the low CPI has put a stop to their recovery," the trader said.
"The CPI-linked long bonds are continuing to rise because of the expected cut in interest rates and because of a tightening supply," he said.
"Yields of the CPI-linked long bonds are already below the 4.1 percent and are getting closer to four percent," he said.
Traders said the strengthening of the shekel beyond its trading band early on Monday had not affected trading of the dollar-linked bonds which closed with price rises.
The shekel streghtened beyond its trading band on rumours that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu would announce a widening of the band later on Monday.

Because the Bank of Israel intervened on a relatively high scale in the market by buying dollars, the shekel's representative rate was fixed lower against the dollar and bakset of foreign currencies on Monday.

The shekel, pegged to a basket of foreign currencies, is allowed to trade in a band of seven percent above or below a diagonal slope designed to devalue the Israeli currency at about six percent a year.
Note: Makams are zero-coupon unlinked certificates with durations of three months to one year. The Bank of Israel issues Makams to absorb liquidity.
($1 = 3.42 shekels)
